mcqs.question: Maintaining nine row sets, nine column sets, and nine box sets of placed digits turns a legality check into what?
options: A single O(1) lookup that replaces all three constraint checks
Three O(1) set-membership lookups, replacing a scan over up to 27 cells
An O(81) scan of the entire board, but only once per cell instead of once per digit tried
A precomputation that only helps if the puzzle has a unique solution
mcqs.explanation: Row, column, and box constraints are three separate checks that each become an O(1) membership test against a maintained set, replacing what would otherwise be scanning up to 9 cells per constraint (up to 27 total) on every single trial digit. It isn't collapsible into one lookup since the three constraints are independent, and it has nothing to do with solution uniqueness.

mcqs.question: A Sudoku solver always fills the first empty cell it finds scanning top-left to bottom-right. Is this correct, and is it fast?
options: Correct, and it's also the fastest possible cell-selection strategy
Incorrect — some valid orderings of cells fail to find existing solutions
Correct, but it can be dramatically slower in practice than a heuristic that picks a more constrained cell first
Incorrect — it violates the row/column/box constraints by construction
mcqs.explanation: Every valid cell-fill order reaches the same solutions eventually, so a fixed top-left scan is correct — but a cell with many legal candidates left explored first branches far more widely than a highly constrained cell would, which can multiply the effective search space enormously on hard puzzles. It doesn't violate any constraint by construction; the issue is purely search efficiency.

mcqs.question: What does the minimum-remaining-values (MRV) heuristic choose to fill next?
options: The empty cell with the fewest legal digits still available
The empty cell closest to the top-left of the board
The empty cell in the row with the most digits already placed
The empty cell with the most legal digits still available
mcqs.explanation: MRV specifically targets the most-constrained cell — the one with the fewest remaining legal options — because it either makes fast, near-forced progress or fails quickly, both of which are better outcomes than exploring a wide-open cell whose real constraints only surface later. Position on the board and how full its row is are unrelated to the heuristic; the most-options cell is the opposite of what MRV picks.

mcqs.question: Adding constraint propagation and MRV cell ordering to a working plain-backtracking Sudoku solver changes what, exactly?
options: It makes previously unsolvable puzzles solvable — plain backtracking cannot solve some valid Sudokus
It changes which solutions are found, since MRV alters the constraint rules themselves
It only matters for puzzles with multiple valid solutions
It typically improves real-world speed substantially, especially on hard puzzles, without changing which solutions exist or are found
mcqs.explanation: Plain backtracking with correct legality checks is already capable of solving any valid Sudoku — propagation and MRV are a performance layer, not a correctness fix, and they don't change the constraint rules or which solutions exist, only how efficiently the search finds them. The speedup is largest on genuinely hard puzzles where a naive cell order would branch widely before failing.

mcqs.question: After placing a digit at (row, col), which parts of the board could possibly now contain a new constraint violation?
options: Only that row, that column, and that 3x3 box — every other row, column, and box is unaffected
The entire board must be rechecked, since any cell could theoretically be affected
Only the row and column, since the box constraint is derived from those two
Only cells adjacent diagonally to the placed digit
mcqs.explanation: A single placement can only create a conflict within the specific row, column, and box that digit belongs to — every other row, column, and box has nothing new to check, so re-validating the entire board wastes work checking regions that provably can't have changed. The box constraint is independent of row/column, not derived from them, and diagonal adjacency isn't a Sudoku rule at all.
